questions.label: Problem 1
questions.statement: State abstraction. Construct a state table for the machine shown in the HW4 handout, then convert it to a FSM diagram. What function does it compute in binary? (The machine, drawn in the HW4 PDF: two half-adder stages in series — the input feeds the first HA; each HA’s carry output C loops back through NOT → MEM → NOT into that HA’s second input; the first HA’s sum S feeds the second HA; the second HA’s sum S is the output.)

questions.label: Problem 2
questions.statement: Multiple realizability. Consider the two SCs in the HW4 handout. What function does each compute in binary? Do they implement the same FSM? Why or why not? Show your work. (The machines, drawn in the HW4 PDF — A: the input splits into both inputs of a first half-adder; its sum S feeds a second half-adder whose other input comes from the two carries joined by an OR gate, then NOT → MEM → NOT, feeding back; the second HA’s sum is the output. B: the input passes through NOT → MEM → NOT in series to the output.)

questions.label: Problem 12
questions.statement: Design a finite-state machine brain that drives the turbot up the zig-zag course: follow the stair-stepped corridor all the way to the goal and keep going until the course offers no way on. The sensor reads the cell ahead (0 = empty, 1 = blocked); each transition outputs the two-bit motor command (11 = forward, 10 = turn right, 01 = turn left, 00 = stop).

questions.label: Problem 13
questions.statement: Three ahead: the goal lies exactly three cells straight ahead of the turbot in an open field. Design a finite-state machine brain that drives the turbot forward onto the goal and stops there. The sensor reads the cell ahead (0 = empty, 1 = blocked); each transition outputs the two-bit motor command (11 = forward, 00 = stop, 10 = turn right, 01 = turn left).

questions.label: Problem 14
questions.statement: Way Finder: the turbot starts at one end of a non-branching maze — a path that never branches and is never wider than one cell across, except on corners where two one-cell-wide paths may intersect. Design a finite-state machine brain that makes its way all the way through any such maze: the layout is not known in advance, so the brain must feel its way with its sensor. Navigation is completed the moment the turbot crosses the goal cell near the far end — it does not need to stop on the goal, and may come to rest once the path finally runs out.
